extracted.intended_audience: judges and patent litigators drafting or using jury instructions in U.S. patent trials
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for patent infringement and invalidity issues used by judges and litigators to guide juries on doctrines such as equivalents, inducement, 35 U.S.C. §271 theories, and prior art/invalidity standards. Focused on U.S. federal patent litigation rules and case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of Equivalents — general principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim element and the [component] [method step] of the [product] [method] is not necessary to find infringement under the doctrine of equivalents; the same accused component/method step may satisfy more than one element of a claim, and two accused components/method steps may satisfy a single claim element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that literal identity is not required for infringement under the doctrine of equivalents; cites Warner-Jenkinson and Graver Tank. Use earlier instructed DOE analysis for elements not subject to limitations discussed below.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of Equivalents — limitation by Prosecution History Estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution history estoppel is determined by the Court; only give the following instruction if the Court has determined estoppel applies as a matter of law. If estoppel applies, the patentee made a representation/argument or amended a claim for reasons related to patentability and has not rebutted the presumption that equivalent subject matter was surrendered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If court has determined estoppel applies, list the specific claim elements (claim-by-claim) to which DOE cannot be applied. For those elements, each must be literally present in the accused product/method to find infringement; remaining elements may be judged under DOE. Cites Festo and Warner-Jenkinson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of Equivalents — limitation by Dedication to the Public
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Court determines that certain subject matter from the patent has been dedicated to the public, the doctrine of equivalents cannot be applied to those listed claim elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dedication to the public is found as a matter of law, identify elements (claim-by-claim) excluded from DOE; those elements must be literally present for infringement. Remaining elements may be evaluated under DOE. Cites SanDisk, Pfizer, PSC Computer Prods., Toro, Johnson & Johnston.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active Inducement to Infringe — prima facie elements
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish active inducement, the plaintiff must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that (1) a single actor is responsible for direct infringement (all components/method steps accused infringe at least one claim), and (2) the defendant actively induced these acts of infringement by the alleged direct infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If both joint infringement and inducement instructions are given, consider presenting them back-to-back to clarify differences and required evidence. Cites 35 U.S.C. §271(b) and cases including Commil, Limelight, Global-Tech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active Inducement — detailed elements (intent/knowledge/willful blindness/direct infringement)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove active inducement, plaintiff must establish by a preponderance that: (1) the defendant aided, instructed, or otherwise acted with the intent to cause acts by the alleged direct infringer that would constitute direct infringement; (2) the defendant knew of the patent, or showed willful blindness to its existence at that time; (3) the defendant knew, or showed willful blindness, that the actions of the alleged direct infringer would infringe at least one claim; and (4) the alleged direct infringer infringed at least one patent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition of willful blindness: (1) defendant subjectively believed there was a high probability a patent existed covering the accused product/method, and (2) defendant took deliberate actions to avoid learning of the patent. Plaintiff must prove all four elements by a preponderance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement under §271(f)(1) — supply of all or a substantial portion abroad
rubrics_metrics.description: To show infringement under Section 271(f)(1), plaintiff must prove by a preponderance that: (1) the product, as intended to be assembled outside the U.S., included all elements of at least one claim; (2) the defendant supplied (or caused to be supplied) components from the U.S. that made up all or a substantial portion of the invention of any one claim; and (3) the defendant specifically intended to induce the combination of the components into a product that would infringe the patent if combined in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'substantial portion' is a quantitative, not qualitative, assessment—export of a single component of a multi-component invention cannot create liability under §271(f)(1). Practice note: §271(f)(1) does not apply to method claims; cites Life Techs., Cardiac Pacemakers, Microsoft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory Infringement — elements
rubrics_metrics.description: To find contributory infringement, plaintiff must prove by a preponderance that: (1) someone other than the defendant directly infringed a claimed invention; (2) the defendant sold, offered for sale, or imported within the U.S. a component of the infringing product or an apparatus for use in the infringing method; (3) the component or apparatus is not a staple article or commodity of commerce capable of substantial non-infringing use; (4) the component or apparatus constitutes a material part of the claimed invention; and (5) the defendant knew that the component was especially made or adapted for use in an infringing product or method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staple article definition: has uses other than as part of the patented product or in the patented method, and those other uses are not occasional/farfetched/impractical/experimental/hypothetical. Defendant's knowledge may be shown by willful blindness (same two-part test). Cites 35 U.S.C. §271(c) and cases including Commil, Global-Tech, Aro, Toshiba.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement under §271(f)(2) — supply of components especially made or adapted for infringing use
rubrics_metrics.description: To show infringement under Section 271(f)(2), plaintiff must prove by a preponderance that: (1) defendant actually supplied the components from the U.S. into a foreign country or caused them to be supplied; (2) defendant knew or should have known that the components were especially made or adapted for use in a product that infringes a claim; (3) those components have no substantial non-infringing use; and (4) defendant intended for the components to be combined into that product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary that the components actually were combined into an infringing product, only that defendant intended them to be combined into a product that would have infringed if combined in the U.S. Cites §271(f)(2), WesternGeco, Microsoft, Cardiac Pacemakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement under §271(g) — import/sale/use of product made by patented process
rubrics_metrics.description: To show infringement under Section 271(g), plaintiff must prove by a preponderance that: (1) defendant imported into the U.S. or, within the U.S., sold/offered for sale/used a product that was made by a process that includes all steps of at least one claim of the patent; (2) the product was made between the issue date of the patent and expiration (or date of trial); and (3) defendant imported/sold/offered/used the product between the issue date and expiration (or date of trial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether evidence establishes the product was 'made by' the claimed process. If product was materially changed by later processes, or is only a trivial/non-essential part of another product, find it was not 'made by' the claimed process. Infringement under §271(g) does not require a single entity to perform the patented process. Cites §271(g) and relevant cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary of Invalidity Defense — burden and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant contends asserted claim(s) are invalid and must prove by clear and convincing evidence that each asserted claim is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury should determine whether each of plaintiff's claims is invalid; identify defendant's specific invalidity contentions and instruct in detail on why defendant alleges invalidity for each asserted claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Art Defined (pre-AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art includes any of the following items received into evidence: any product/method publicly known or used by others in the U.S. before the claimed invention was invented; any product/method that was in public use or on sale in the U.S. before the Cutoff Date; any patents that issued before the Cutoff Date; any publications having dates of public accessibility before the Cutoff Date; and any product/method made by anyone in the U.S. before the date of invention where the claimed invention was not later abandoned, suppressed, or concealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. §102. Practice note: identify for the jury issues such as date/public availability when parties dispute a reference's status as prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Art Defined (AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art includes: anything patented, described in a printed publication, in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public anywhere in the world before the effective filing date of the claim(s); and anything described in a patent or application published or deemed published naming another inventor and filed before the effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists exceptions: a disclosure made one year or less before the effective filing date by the inventor (or from the inventor) need not be prior art; other statutory exceptions for derived disclosures or common ownership apply. Cites 35 U.S.C. §102 (AIA) and §100(i); Helsinn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Art — effect of whether reference was considered by the USPTO
rubrics_metrics.description: Regardless of whether a particular prior art reference was considered by the Patent Examiner during prosecution, defendant must prove invalidity by clear and convincing evidence; this burden never changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice note: If the PTO did not have all material facts, the challenger's burden may be easier to sustain; jury may be instructed to evaluate whether evidence is materially new compared to what PTO considered. Cites Microsoft v. i4i and related decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity of Independent and Dependent Claims — how to evaluate
rubrics_metrics.description: There are independent claims (do not refer to other claims) and dependent claims (refer to at least one other claim). A dependent claim includes all elements recited in it and all elements of the claim to which it refers. You must evaluate invalidity for each asserted claim separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if an independent claim is invalid, dependent claims that depend from it are not automatically invalid — decide validity claim-by-claim. However, if you find a dependent claim invalid, you must find the independent claim from which it depends also invalid. Provide examples and identify differences between specific independent/dependent claims. Cites Federal Circuit authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person of Ordinary Skill in the Art (POSITA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Invalidity is determined from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art in the field of the claimed invention as of the time of the invention/effective filing date; prior art must be evaluated from that perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 35 U.S.C. §103, KSR, and other cases. Jury should apply the understanding a POSITA would have had at the relevant date when assessing obviousness and interpretation of prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation — newness requirement and single-reference test
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove anticipation, defendant must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the claimed invention is not new. To anticipate a claim, each element in the claim must be present in a single item of prior art and arranged or combined in the same way as recited in the claim; you may not combine two or more items of prior art to find anticipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider what a POSITA would have understood from the particular publication/patent/etc. If inherent anticipation is alleged, instruct on inherency: a missing element is inherently present if it necessarily results from the prior art reference; necessity must be proven by clear and convincing evidence. Evidence outside the reference (including testing) may be used to show inherency. Cites many Federal Circuit authorities and practice note on inherency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Public Knowledge (pre-AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant contends the claims are invalid because the invention was publicly known by others in the U.S. before the Cutoff Date (pre-AIA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there's a factual dispute about date of invention or priority, instruct jury on how to determine the Cutoff Date. Patent claim is invalid if invention was publicly known by others in the U.S. before it was invented by the patentee. Cites 35 U.S.C. §102(a) (pre-AIA) and case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Public Knowledge (AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant contends claims are invalid because the claimed invention was available to the public before the effective filing date (AIA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If factual issues about exception to prior art (e.g., disclosures within one year by inventor or derived disclosures, or common ownership) exist, instruct jury on §102(b) and (c) exceptions as needed. Cites 35 U.S.C. §102(a)(1) (AIA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Public Use (pre-AIA) — public use and readiness for patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant contends claims are invalid because the invention was publicly used by others in the U.S. before the relevant Cutoff Date or more than one year before the patentee filed. An invention was publicly used if an embodiment was both (1) accessible to the public or commercially exploited in the U.S., and (2) ready for patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors for public use: nature of activity, public access, confidentiality obligations, commercial exploitation (even if specifics kept secret), circumstances of testing/experimentation; absence of steps to conceal is evidence of public use. Secret use by a third party is not public unless public or employees had access. 'Ready for patenting' means reduced to practice or having drawings/descriptions enabling a POSITA to make/use the invention. Reduction to practice requires constructing an embodiment or performing the process and determining it would work for its intended purpose. Cites pre-AIA §102(a),(b) and numerous cases (Pfaff, Am. Seating, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Public Use (AIA) — worldwide public use
rubrics_metrics.description: Under AIA, defendant contends the claimed invention was in public use anywhere in the world before the effective filing date, making the claim invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An invention was in public use if it was accessible to the public or commercially exploited anywhere in the world. Relevant factors mirror pre-AIA public use factors (nature of activity, public access, confidentiality, commercial exploitation, testing circumstances). If factual issues concern disclosures within one year or derived disclosures/common ownership, instruct jury on §102(b) and (c) exceptions as needed.
